title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 6
summary:
The first law says energy is conserved; it does *not* say which direction a process can go. The **second law** supplies that direction. Heat flows from hot to cold on its own, never the reverse without help; a falling weight stirs water warm, but a warm cup never cools to lift a weight. Energy has **quality** as well as quantity, and every real process degrades it.

The law is framed around devices exchanging heat with **thermal reservoirs** (bodies so large their temperature doesn't change). A **heat engine** takes heat $Q_H$ from a hot reservoir, produces net work $W_{net}$, and rejects $Q_L$ to a cold one. Its **thermal efficiency** is $\eta_{th} = W_{net}/Q_H = 1 - Q_L/Q_H$. The **Kelvin–Planck statement** says $\eta_{th}$ can never reach 1: some heat must always be rejected. You cannot build an engine that turns *all* its heat input into work.

Run in reverse, the device is a **refrigerator** or **heat pump**, moving heat from cold to hot using work input. Their performance is a **coefficient of performance (COP)** — and because the useful effect is large relative to the work, COP is usually greater than 1. For a fridge $COP_R = Q_L/W_{net}$; for a heat pump $COP_{HP} = Q_H/W_{net}$; and they differ by exactly one, $COP_{HP} = COP_R + 1$. The **Clausius statement** says no device can move heat from cold to hot with *no* work input.

The gold standard is the **Carnot cycle** — a reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes. **Carnot's principles** state that (1) no real engine between two reservoirs can beat a reversible one, and (2) all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the *same* efficiency, set only by the reservoir temperatures. This gives the famous limits: $\eta_{th,rev} = 1 - T_L/T_H$, with temperatures in **kelvin**. These are ceilings — real devices fall short because of friction, finite temperature differences, and other irreversibilities.

The practical use: compute a device's actual efficiency/COP from the heat and work, compare it against the Carnot limit for the same reservoir temperatures, and judge how good it is — or spot an impossible claim (efficiency above the Carnot value).

equations.name: Thermal efficiency of a heat engine
equations.useWhen: Any heat engine (power plant, car engine). Use the $Q$ form when heats are given, the $W/Q_H$ form when work and input heat are given.
equations.note: $W_{net} = Q_H - Q_L$ by the first law over a cycle. Always $\eta_{th} < 1$.

equations.name: COP of a refrigerator
equations.useWhen: A refrigerator or air conditioner — the desired effect is *removing* heat $Q_L$ from the cold space.
equations.note: Can exceed 1. The desired output is the cooling, $Q_L$.

equations.name: COP of a heat pump
equations.useWhen: A heat pump heating a space — the desired effect is *delivering* heat $Q_H$. Same hardware as a fridge, different goal.
equations.note: $COP_{HP} = COP_R + 1$, so it is always greater than 1.

equations.name: Carnot (reversible) efficiency
equations.useWhen: Finding the maximum possible efficiency between two reservoirs, or checking whether a claimed engine is feasible ($\eta_{th} \le \eta_{th,rev}$).
equations.note: Temperatures MUST be absolute (K). The substitution $Q_L/Q_H = T_L/T_H$ holds only for a reversible device.

equations.name: Carnot COPs (reversible limits)
equations.useWhen: The best possible COP for a refrigerator/heat pump between two temperatures — the benchmark a real unit is measured against.
equations.note: Temperatures in K. The smaller the temperature gap $T_H - T_L$, the higher the COP.

glossary.definition: Processes proceed in a preferred direction and energy quality always degrades; not everything allowed by the first law actually happens.
A body large enough to absorb or supply heat with no change in temperature (oceans, the atmosphere, a furnace). Source = supplies heat; sink = absorbs it.
A device that converts part of a heat input $Q_H$ into net work $W_{net}$, rejecting the remainder $Q_L$ to a sink.
Fraction of heat input converted to work, $\eta_{th} = W_{net}/Q_H = 1 - Q_L/Q_H$.
A device using work to move heat from a cold space to a warm one; performance measured by $COP_R = Q_L/W_{net}$.
Same as a refrigerator but the goal is heating the warm space; $COP_{HP} = Q_H/W_{net} = COP_R + 1$.
Desired heat transfer divided by work input; can be (and usually is) greater than 1.
No heat engine can convert all the heat it receives into work — some must be rejected ($\eta_{th} < 1$).
No device can transfer heat from a cooler to a hotter body without work input.
A reversible process can be undone leaving no trace; real processes are irreversible due to friction, fast expansion, finite $\Delta T$ heat transfer, mixing.
The ideal reversible cycle: two isothermal and two adiabatic (isentropic) processes; sets the efficiency ceiling.
(1) No engine beats a reversible one between the same reservoirs; (2) all reversible engines between the same reservoirs have equal efficiency, fixed by $T_H, T_L$.

tips: **Temperatures in the Carnot formulas MUST be in kelvin.** Using °C gives nonsense. This is the number-one second-law error.
**Refrigerator vs. heat pump = same machine, different desired output.** Cold side wanted → $COP_R$ ($Q_L$ on top). Hot side wanted → $COP_{HP}$ ($Q_H$ on top). They differ by exactly 1.
**Carnot values are ceilings, not predictions.** A real device gives $\eta_{th} \le \eta_{th,rev}$ and $COP \le COP_{rev}$. If a claim exceeds the Carnot limit, it's impossible.
**$Q_L/Q_H = T_L/T_H$ only for reversible devices.** For a real engine use the *energy* ratio $Q_L/Q_H$ from the data, not the temperature ratio.
**Smaller temperature gap → better COP.** Heat pumps and fridges work best when $T_H - T_L$ is small; this is why heat pumps lose efficiency on very cold days.
**Over a cycle, $W_{net} = Q_H - Q_L$.** The device returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U_{cycle} = 0$ and the first law gives net work = net heat.
